Persistent atrial fibrillation in older adults: Comparison of seven models and development of a gradient boosting machine classifier in a single-center observational study.

This single-center observational study of 572 older adults compared seven classification models for identifying persistent atrial fibrillation and selected a gradient boosting machine classifier as the best performer. The work also characterizes clinical correlates of persistent AF in this population and interprets the chosen model's predictors. It is a clinical modeling study with modest sample size and limited generalizability.

Machine-learning-assisted multi-omics profiling identifies CALB1 as a subtype-associated regulator of PI3K/AKT signaling and malignant progression in non-small cell lung cancer.

This study uses a machine-learning-assisted multi-omics framework to identify subtype-associated regulators in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), nominating CALB1 as a candidate. The authors then functionally characterize CALB1, showing it is associated with molecular subtypes, regulates PI3K/AKT signaling, and contributes to malignant progression. The work combines computational biomarker discovery with experimental validation to address the gap between computationally nominated targets and functional evidence.

A multispecies foundation model for genome function prediction, gene annotation and sequence design.

The authors present Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3), a cross-kingdom genomic foundation model pre-trained on over 128,000 genomes with sequence contexts up to 1 Mb and post-trained on 16,262 functional tracks. NTv3 provides a single backbone for genome function prediction, gene annotation, and controllable DNA sequence generation across phylogenetically diverse species, extending genomic foundation models beyond a few well-characterized organisms.

Species phylogenetics using intraprotein residue dependence inferred with protein foundation models.

This preprint proposes using protein foundation models to infer phylogenetic relationships from intraprotein residue dependencies rather than traditional alignment-based substitution models that assume site independence. The authors compare evolutionary scale models (ESM) that analyze individual sequences with MSA Transformer models that analyze alignments, extracting residue attention matrices and sequence attention matrices as phylogenetic signals. The approach represents a methodological shift toward leveraging deep learning-derived structural and co-evolutionary information for species phylogenetics.

A compact generative language model learns the compositional grammar of phase-separating proteins.

The authors trained a compact generative language model (~17M parameters) specifically on phase-separating intrinsically disordered proteins, showing that a small model can learn the compositional sequence grammar that promotes liquid-liquid phase separation. This suggests that LLPS-prone disordered proteins have distinctive compositional biases that general-purpose, folded-protein-rich language models may miss, and that targeted small models can capture them efficiently.

Building from the ground up: augmentation strategies to improve protein language model performance on protein sets.

This preprint investigates how protein language models (pLMs) perform when trained on small, limited datasets—a common bottleneck in biology—and tests data augmentation strategies to improve predictive performance. The authors find that narrowing the distribution of protein-protein complexes in a limited dataset allows an order-of-magnitude reduction in data requirements, and they characterize how pLMs learn from suboptimal data. The work offers practical augmentation guidance for building better protein ML models with scarce experimental data.

Viral host assignment across the tree of life with VHAMSTeR.

VHAMSTeR is a new classification framework that predicts the host organism of viral sequences across five broad categories (prokaryote, animal, plant, fungi, protist). It combines fine-tuned genomic language model embeddings with explicit biological features such as genome architecture and protein homology, and substantially outperforms existing host prediction methods for both DNA (MCC > 0.91) and RNA (MCC > 0.69) viruses.

LongVerse: verified AI agents for Nanopore and PacBio DNA methylation analysis.

LongVerse is an AI agent system that converts a single English sentence into haplotype-resolved DNA methylation calls from Nanopore or PacBio reads, with agents that read data and configure a pinned pipeline rather than writing code. On the HG002 reference genome, agent and human expert outputs were byte-identical (r = 1.000) and agreed well with bisulfite sequencing (r = 0.943 and 0.884), at a cost of $0.12–$0.54 per run. The work demonstrates verification of agent outputs against an independent measurement rather than rubric or LLM-judge scoring.

Germline dependence in protein language model retrieval of adaptive immune receptors.

This study benchmarks protein language models against classical sequence-comparison methods for retrieving antigen-specific B- and T-cell receptors. Using CDR3 sequences alone, classical methods like BLOSUM62 and Levenshtein consistently outperformed general protein language models (e.g., ESM2) by 7-12 percentage points in retrieval accuracy, and only a few receptor-specific models matched or exceeded classical approaches. The findings suggest that germline-encoded sequence similarity, captured well by simple alignment-based methods, remains a strong baseline that general PLMs do not reliably surpass for immune receptor retrieval.
